content.text: Specificity isn't a score. It's three counts (IDs, classes, types) compared column by column, so no number of classes ever beats one more ID. The belief: specificity is a points total, often taught as 100 per ID, 10 per class and 1 per element. Stack enough classes and you'll outscore an ID. And when a rule loses anyway,
It's an understandable model, because it gives the right answer in most everyday fights: an ID beats two classes, a class beats an element, and the more specific selector wins.

How to apply it in your project
Put one statement at the top of your entry stylesheet, such as

content.text: Import resets, vendor CSS and legacy styles into the early layers. Your own component styles then win by layer, not by selector length.
Use classes for styling and keep IDs for anchors and labels. Where an ID selector must stay, wrap it in
. Each one either becomes a layer decision or gets a comment explaining why it must stay, which is what MDN recommends when it can't be avoided.

items.text: Specificity is ID-CLASS-TYPE, compared column by column: one more ID beats any number of classes.
The cascade checks importance, inline styles and layers before specificity, and order of appearance breaks the last tie.
Inherited values never compete with a rule that matches the element itself.
Later layers beat earlier ones regardless of specificity, and unlayered styles beat every layer.
